He said they were interested. She said they had reviewed the proposal. He told me they would confirm on Friday. She asked whether we could send the numbers.
So how did it go? Did they say yes?
Not exactly. He said they were interested, but that they could not commit before they had seen the audit report.
So they approved it in principle.
That is close, and I would put it slightly differently. Interested is not approved. I do not want to put words in his mouth: the caveat was the whole sentence.
Fair. Did he say when the audit report lands?
He told me it would be ready by the end of the month, and he asked whether we could send the migration plan before that.
And what is the takeaway for the board?
That the takeaway is a date, not a decision. I will send a recap tonight and I will read the sentence back to him tomorrow, so nobody has to paraphrase me either.
He said they were interested, but that they could not commit yet.
He asked whether we could send the migration plan first.
That is close, and I would put it slightly differently.
Let me read that back to you before I take it to my team.
If I have got any of this wrong, please correct me before Friday.

The most expensive thing I have ever done in this job was report a meeting slightly wrong. Not a lie. Slightly wrong. The client had said they were comfortable with the timeline, and what I told my own team was that they had approved the timeline, and those are not the same sentence. Comfortable is a feeling. Approved is a decision. Six weeks later we had built to a date nobody had actually signed off, and when it came apart the client was completely right and I had nothing to stand on. What I do now is boring and it has never failed me. I write down the sentence while they are still saying it, in their words, and if I am going to repeat it to anybody I read it back to them first. It takes eleven seconds and it has saved me from that conversation about four times since.

There is a thing that happens in every second meeting and nobody names it. Somebody says, so what you are saying is, and then says something you did not say. Usually it is not malicious. They are compressing, and the compression drops the caveat. The problem is that from that moment on the room is working with their version, not yours, and if you let it go once it becomes the record. What I have learned to say, and I say it gently, is: that is close, and I would put it slightly differently. Then I say my version. Nobody has ever taken offence. And the reverse is just as important. When I am the one summarising somebody else, I say, tell me if I have got this wrong, and about a third of the time they do tell me, and that third is where the whole deal lives.
